mcqs.question: Why is a pastebin's read:write ratio typically lower than a URL shortener's?
options: Pastes are read by a bot crawler on every request, inflating shortener numbers instead
Most pastes are viewed a handful of times rather than clicked repeatedly by a wide audience, unlike a shared link
Pastebins do not support public visibility
Object storage cannot serve high read volumes
mcqs.explanation: A typical paste (a snippet shared with a few teammates) gets read only a few times, unlike a shortened link that can be clicked by a wide, ongoing audience — so the average ratio is lower, even though a rare viral paste spikes it. Object storage handles high read volume fine; visibility settings are unrelated to this ratio.

mcqs.question: Why should paste content live in object storage rather than directly in a database row?
options: Databases cannot store text data at all
Object storage is always faster for every read, regardless of size
Large, variable-size blobs in the DB crowd out its buffer cache and cost more per byte than purpose-built object storage
It is required by most database licensing terms
mcqs.explanation: Storing large, size-variable content directly in the database bloats rows and evicts other frequently-accessed data from its cache, and object storage is cheaper per byte for this use case. Databases can store text fine for small values; object storage isn't universally faster for tiny reads; there's no licensing rule involved.

mcqs.question: What problem does request coalescing solve during a viral-paste read stampede that a plain cache-aside layer does not?
options: It prevents the paste from expiring early
It reduces the object's storage cost
It stops multiple concurrent cache misses for the same key from each independently re-fetching from the object store
It encrypts the paste content in transit
mcqs.explanation: Without coalescing, every concurrent request that misses the cache in the same instant issues its own redundant fetch to the object store; coalescing merges those into a single fetch shared by all waiters. It has nothing to do with expiry timing, storage cost, or encryption.

mcqs.question: What's the main downside of storing paste content inline in the same database row as its metadata?
options: It makes the paste's short code longer
Large, variable-size rows evict the working set of small metadata rows from the DB's cache and cost more than object storage per byte
It prevents pastes from having an expiry
It makes the API surface larger
mcqs.explanation: Mixing large variable-size content with small metadata in one table hurts cache efficiency for the metadata and costs more per byte than object storage built for blobs. It has no effect on code length, expiry support, or the API's shape.
